title: The Honest Woodcutter and Akbar
summary: Akbar meets an old woodcutter singing joyfully despite poverty. Birbal shows the Emperor why peace of mind cannot be bought with an imperial treasury.
full_text:
During an early morning stroll along the outskirts of Agra, Emperor Akbar and Birbal observed an elderly woodcutter named Kashi, clad in rags, chopping dry logs with an iron axe. Sweat poured down the old man's brow, yet he whistled merrily and sang folk songs with genuine joy.

Akbar, who had spent the previous night tossing sleeplessly over border treaties and treasury shortages, stopped his horse in wonder: 'Look at that peasant, Birbal. He works twelve hours in the blistering heat for barely four copper coins a day, yet he sings as if he were the lord of paradise! I am ruler of Hindustan with rooms full of diamonds, yet I cannot sleep for an hour without anxiety. Why is he happier than an emperor?'

Birbal smiled: 'Sire, his wealth is invisible. He possesses the three jewels that monarchs often lose: contentment, honest labor, and the absence of greed. If you wish to test this, let us give him a small taste of greed, and observe what happens.'

That evening, Birbal arranged for a palace courier to leave a leather purse containing ninety-nine gold mohurs upon the woodcutter's porch, with a note: 'A gift for an honest laborer.'

When Kashi found the purse, his eyes widened with shock. He counted the coins: 'One, two, three... ninety-eight, ninety-nine!'

He counted again. Ninety-nine!

A strange restlessness seized the old man's heart. 'Ninety-nine is an incomplete number! Why did the benefactor not give me one hundred? I must earn one more gold coin to make it a full, round hundred!'

From that night, Kashi stopped singing. He stopped laughing. He worked eighteen hours a day, starving himself and cutting wood till his hands bled, obsessed with saving one gold coin. He hid the ninety-nine coins under his floor, waking up every hour in terror that thieves were digging beneath his hut. His cheerfulness vanished; his face grew haggard and suspicious.

A month later, Akbar and Birbal rode past the woodcutter's clearing. Kashi was scowling fiercely, cursing at his axe, his face dark with misery.

Akbar was astonished: 'What happened to his joy?'

Birbal explained: 'Sire, he has entered the trap of the ninety-nine! Before, he lived in the present, thankful for his daily bread. Now, he lives in fear of losing what he has and longing for the one coin he lacks. Greed is a fire that consumes peace, whether in a peasant's hut or an imperial palace.'

Akbar retrieved the gold, granted Kashi a comfortable monthly pension that preserved his peace without feeding avarice, and thanked Birbal for the profound lesson.
moral: Lição de moral: Wit beats power
